```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("workshops", "workshop-01", "01_clean_data.R"))
dev <- readRDS(here("data", "processed", "global_development_clean.rds"))
```

# Project structure and import

**1.1**

```{r}
raw <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "global_development_intro.csv"))
```

**1.2**

```{r}
dim(raw)
```

**1.3** One row is one country in one year. Each of the 19 countries is observed in each of the 21 years 2000–2020, so 19 × 21 = 399 rows. This is panel data.

# Measurement scales

**2.1** `region` is nominal (names, no order). `income_group` is ordinal (ordered categories with unequal gaps). `year` is interval (equal one-year steps, no true zero). `internet_use` is ratio (0% really means nobody).

**2.2**

```{r}
levels(dev$income_group)
```

**2.3** The numbers 1–7 are only labels. Their average has no meaning: there is no "region 3.4". For a nominal variable, report counts or shares instead.

# Missing values

**3.1**

```{r}
colSums(is.na(raw))
```

**3.2**

```{r}
dev |> filter(is.na(gdp_growth_pct)) |> count(year)
```

**3.3** Growth compares a year with the year before. In 2000, the first year, there is no year before, so growth cannot be computed. These NAs are correct and expected, not a data problem.

**3.4** Too **high**. The countries that drop out are the ones with the lowest values, so the remaining average is pulled up. This is **missing not at random (MNAR)**: whether a value is missing depends on the value itself. It creates bias, and a bigger sample does not fix it.

# Cleaning and dates

**4.1**

```{r}
north_africa <- dev |>
  filter(country_short %in% c("Egypt", "Morocco", "Tunisia")) |>
  select(country_short, year, youth_unemployment)
north_africa
```

**4.2**

```{r}
start <- ymd("2000-01-01")
end   <- ymd("2020-12-31")
end - start
```

# Reshaping

**5.1**

```{r}
north_africa |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = youth_unemployment)
```

**5.2** `ggplot()` needs **long** data: one column for the x-axis (year), one for the y-axis (value), one for the colour (country). The wide table is easier for humans to read and compare across years, which makes it a good format for a report table.

# Descriptive statistics

**6.1 and 6.2**

```{r}
dev |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2020)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(mean_internet = mean(internet_use),
            median_internet = median(internet_use))
```

**6.3** In 2000 most countries were near 0% and a few rich ones were far higher: a long **right** tail pulled the mean (9.8) far above the median (2.8). By 2020 most countries had caught up, and the leaders could not go above 100%. The values bunched near the top with a tail on the **left**, and the mean and median became almost equal. The skewness changes sign, from about +1.4 to about −1.0:

```{r}
skewness <- function(x) mean(((x - mean(x)) / sd(x))^3)
dev |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2020)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(skew_internet = skewness(internet_use))
```

**6.4**

```{r}
dev |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(median_life = median(life_expectancy)) |>
  arrange(desc(median_life))
```

**6.5** The **standard deviation** says how much individual countries differ from each other. The **standard error** says how much an *average* would change if we drew a different random sample. The SE gets smaller as the sample gets bigger; the SD does not.

# Transformations

**7.1**

```{r}
dev_z <- dev |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(youth_z = (youth_unemployment - mean(youth_unemployment)) / sd(youth_unemployment)) |>
  ungroup()

dev_z |> filter(year == 2020) |> arrange(desc(youth_z)) |> select(country_short, youth_z)
```

**7.2** In 2020, South Africa's youth unemployment is far above the average of the 19 countries. It is almost three times the usual gap between a country and that average. In other words, it is an extreme case even in this group.

**7.3**

```{r}
dev |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  summarise(r_raw = cor(gdp_per_capita_ppp, life_expectancy),
            r_log = cor(log_gdp_per_capita, life_expectancy))
```

**7.4** Correlation measures how close points are to a **straight line**. Life expectancy rises fast as income grows from low levels, then flattens. On the raw dollar scale that is a curve; on the log scale it becomes close to a straight line, so the correlation is higher.

# Visualisation

**8.1**

```{r}
p_na <- ggplot(north_africa, aes(x = year, y = youth_unemployment, colour = country_short)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Youth unemployment in North Africa, 2000-2020",
       x = NULL, y = "Youth unemployment (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
p_na
```

**8.2**

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
life_2020 <- filter(dev, year == 2020)
ggplot(life_2020, aes(x = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 6, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "bins = 6") + theme_minimal()
ggplot(life_2020, aes(x = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "bins = 12") + theme_minimal()
```

With 6 bins the shape looks smooth and simple. With 12 bins and only 19 countries, many bins hold 0 or 1 country and the shape looks jagged. The data did not change; only the picture did. Always try more than one bin count.

**8.3**

```{r}
ggsave(here("outputs", "figures", "w1_north_africa_youth.png"), p_na,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

# Reproducibility

**9.1** Answers vary. Common problems: a package not loaded at the top of the file, an object created in the Console but not in the file, or a path typed as `C:/Users/...` instead of with `here()`.

**9.2** Examples: editing the raw CSV by hand; saving a figure with right-click instead of `ggsave()`; using an absolute path; creating objects in the Console that the file depends on; not recording package versions (`renv`).

# Extension

**10.1** Replace `geom_text(...)` with `ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = country_short), size = 3)`. It moves labels so they do not overlap.

**10.2**

```{r}
dev |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2020)) |>
  select(country_short, year, youth_unemployment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = youth_unemployment, names_prefix = "y") |>
  mutate(change = y2020 - y2000) |>
  arrange(change)
```
